Joint Channel, Data and Radar Parameter Estimation for AFDM Systems in Doubly-Dispersive Channels

Kuranage Roche Rayan Ranasinghe    Hyeon Seok Rou    Giuseppe Thadeu Freitas de Abreu    Takumi Takahashi    Kenta Ito ††thanks: Kuranage Roche Rayan Ranasinghe, Hyeon Seok Rou and Giuseppe Thadeu Freitas de Abreu are with the School of Computer Science and Engineering, Constructor University (previously Jacobs University Bremen), Campus Ring 1, 28759 Bremen, Germany (emails: [kranasinghe, hrou, gabreu]@constructor.university). Takumi Takahashi and Kenta Ito are with the Graduate School of Engineering, Osaka University, Suita 565-0871, Japan (emails: [takahashi@, k-ito@wcs.]comm.eng.osaka-u.ac.jp). Part of this work was presented at the 2024 IEEE 21st Consumer Communications & Networking Conference (CCNC) [1].
Abstract

We propose new schemes for joint channel and data estimation (JCDE) and radar parameter estimation (RPE) in doubly-dispersive channels, such that integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) is enabled by user equipment (UE) independently performing JCDE, and base stations (BSs) performing RPE. The contributed JCDE and RPE schemes are designed for waveforms known to perform well in doubly-dispersive channels, under a unified model that captures the features of either legacy orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM), state-of-the-art (SotA) orthogonal time frequency space (OTFS), and next-generation affine frequency division multiplexing (AFDM) systems. The proposed JCDE algorithm is based on a Bayesian parametric bilinear Gaussian belief propagation (PBiGaBP) framework first proposed for OTFS and here shown to apply to all aforementioned waveforms, while the RPE scheme is based on a new probabilistic data association (PDA) approach incorporating a Bernoulli-Gaussian denoising, optimized via expectation maximization (EM). Simulation results demonstrate that JCDE in AFDM systems utilizing a single pilot per block significantly outperforms the SotA alternative even if the latter is granted a substantial power advantage. Similarly, the AFDM-based RPE scheme is found to outperform the OTFS-based approach, as well as the sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) technique, regardless of the waveform used.

Index Terms: 
ISAC, AFDM, OTFS, JCDE, PBiGaBP, PDA, EM, RPE, Bayesian Inference.

I Introduction

The building blocks of communications and radar systems have been traditionally designed separately and assumed to utilize orthogonal resources. Integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) 11 1 Also commonly referred to as joint communication and sensing (JCAS) or joint communications and radar (JCR). [2, 3, 4, 5], a recently-emerged technology seen by many as a key driver of future mobile communication systems, challenges that established concept by considering the simultaneous provision of radar and communications functionalities under the same architecture, having the advantages of more efficient use of resources, lower power consumption, decreased hardware costs and the potential for wide market penetration [6, 7, 8]. While different perspectives on ISAC exists, each with a particular paradigm – e.g.e.g. co-existence of communications and radar systems [9] or dual-function approaches [10] – the focus of this manuscript is on enabling sensing functionalities under wireless communications systems, also referred to as communication-centric ISAC.

Staying true to the integrative aspect of the proposition, earlier contributions to ISAC focused on schemes employing existing communications waveforms. In particular, many methods found in current literature seek to take advantage of certain features of channel estimation – especially in higher frequency bands where less scattering, higher resolution and domain-specific sparsity enable the estimation of individual channel paths – to incorporate radar-like functionalities, such as the estimation of radar parameters from echoes of the transmit signal [11, 12, 13, 14, 15].

Examples of the latter are techniques based on the orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) waveform [13, 14] which, however, indicated that the high inter-carrier interference (ICI) can be a bottleneck that reduces robustness to high Doppler shifts present in doubly-dispersive environments, leading to severe degradation of performance. This factor alone, introduced by the channel diagonals spreading into a decaying band [16], severely hinders the use of OFDM in high mobility scenarios [17], as envisioned for 6G systems.

Another potential candidate for the ISAC paradigm is the orthogonal time frequency space (OTFS) waveform, which was originally proposed in [18] as a novel two-dimensional (2D) modulation scheme that embeds information directly on the delay-Doppler (DD) domain. Since the DD domain has a direct parallel to common radar processing framework, OTFS was quite popular at its inception, attracting much work that demonstrated its effectiveness for ISAC [11, 12, 13, 15, 14]. However, besides the significantly higher implementation complexity compared to OFDM, which is inherent to its 2D modulation approach, another limitation of OTFS is that it does not achieve the optimal diversity order in doubly-dispersive channels [19].

In response to the above, affine frequency division multiplexing (AFDM) has recently emerged as a strong candidate for ISAC [20, 21, 22, 23], gaining much attention thanks to its robust communications performance in high mobility scenarios and its ability to achieve optimal diversity order in doubly-dispersive channels. The key idea of AFDM is to employ the discrete affine Fourier transform (DAFT) to generate multiple orthogonal chirps that are then used to modulate the transmit signal. Since AFDM is otherwise similar to OFDM in structure, it does not suffer from the high modulation complexity of OTFS, and since the chirp parameters of AFDM can be optimized to match the maximum Doppler shift of the doubly-dispersive channel, a full DD representation of the channel can be achieved, giving the approach remarkable robustness to high mobility and/or frequency.

It has been in fact demonstrated that AFDM has a superior bit error rate (BER) performance compared to OFDM, achieving also BERs comparable to OTFS while requiring lower overhead for channel estimation [22] as a result of the one-dimensional (1D) null-guard band required, as opposed to that of OTFS, which is 2D. In turn, evidence that AFDM can be effectively utilized for ISAC has also been given, for instance in [21] where a simple matched-filter (MF) approach was suggested. Building on the latter, an improved AFDM-based monostatic ISAC system with inherent adaptation to self-interference mitigation was also designed in [23], albeit at the expense of a significant increase in computational complexity due to the exhaustive maximum likelihood (ML) grid search required for the radar parameter estimation (RPE) procedure.

One aspect of the ISAC concept that was often overlooked, and which recently has been addressed more frontally, however, is the impact of pilot overhead onto the overall approach, when designing the appropriate frame structure for optimum data decoding at a user equipment (UE) being served. It has been shown in [22], for instance, that a major advantage of AFDM over OFDM and OTFS is the lighter requirement in the number of pilots, which in turn can be taken advantage of by enabling the base station (BS) to perform RPE without expensive self-interference cancellation (SIC) techniques. The trend to reduce pilot overhead suggests, therefore, the adoption of joint channel and data estimation (JCDE) technology, which has been shown to be very effective in allowing efficient channel estimation with very few pilots22 2 The embedded channel estimation method proposed in [22] requires a single pilot, but surrounded by a null-guard interval, such that the fraction of the AFDM frame dedicated to payload is affected not just by the sole pilot but also the additional power that can be allocated to it. and under strenuous conditions [24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 1, 29], significantly reduce the overhead of coherent wireless systems. One example of the latter is the Bayesian bilinear inference (BBI) JCDE scheme for OFDM systems proposed in [28], which was shown to have the ability of handling channel aging and to entirely remove the need of pilots in favor of adequate coding at an equivalent rate. Another is the work in [1], where a Bayesian parametric bilinear Gaussian belief propagation (PBiGaBP) JCDE scheme for OTFS systems was proposed, which was shown to asymptotically approach the idealized scheme where perfect channel state information (CSI) knowledge is available.

In view of all the above, we propose in this paper a combined and generalized JCDE-enabled ISAC solution for systems utilizing signals known to cope well with doubly-dispersive channels, including OFDM, OTFS and AFDM. The proposed solution comprises of two main contributions. The first is a new JCDEmechanism, designed with basis on the Bayesian PBiGaBP originally proposed for OTFS waveforms in [1], which is shown to function also for the other modulation schemes under the general doubly-dispersive channel model developed in [16]. Comparisons of the state-of-the-art (SotA) OTFS and the contributed AFDM methods against a genie-aided linear Gaussian belief propagation (GaBP) benchmark scheme, in which perfect CSI is assumed, demonstrate that the proposed solution under AFDM achieves the same performance of the OTFS SotA, both of which also closely approach the idealistic benchmark, indicating that there is no penalty for the reduced modulation complexity advantage obtained when utilizing AFDM instead of OTFS, and that the proposed scheme is effective in reducing pilot overhead.

The second contribution is a new RPE scheme based on the vectorized probabilistic data association (PDA) approach [25, 28] incorporating a Bernoulli-Gaussian denoiser tuned via expectation maximization (EM) [30] which quickly converges to the appropriate distribution parameters. Compared to the SotA alternative adapted from [31], which is designed around the sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) algorithm, the contributed method is shown to outperform the latter over any of the relevant waveforms, namely, OFDM, OTFS in [31] and AFDM. The technique also has an inherent and substantial computational cost advantage over ML-based SotA alternatives such as those in [22] and [23].

The contributions of the article are summarized as follows:

  • •

    In Section II, we concisely revise the unified OFDM, OTFS and AFDMdoubly-dispersive channel model from [16], such that message-passing receivers for such waveforms can be designed under a common structure.

  • •

    Taking advantage of the former, we propose in Section III a PBiGaBP-based scheme for JCDE, which applies to all the aforementioned waveforms.

  • •

    We show that even if a single pilot per block is used, the proposed JCDE-AFDM system significantly outperforms both the OFDM and OTFS alternatives [1], as well as the AFDM method in[23], even when the latter is granted a substantial power advantage.

  • •

    Finally, in Section IV-B, a novel PDA-based technique for RPE in doubly-dispersive channels is proposed, which in addition to enabling monostatic implementation for AFDM systems without requiring full-duplex (FD) technology, is shown to outperform the SotA of [31] for both OTFS and AFDM waveforms.

II System Model

We follow [23] and consider an ISAC scenario composed of a single-antenna33 3 Both proposed algorithms can be extended straightforwardly to a single-input multiple-output (SIMO) case, with some modifications due to spatial filtering/interference cancellation for which isotropic beamforming as done in [32] could be used. Generalization to the multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) case is also possible, but requires the formulation and solution of a non-trivial transmit (TX) and receive (RX) beamforming optimization problem. Such contribution falls outside the scope of this article and will be offered in a follow-up work. BS transmitting in downlink and taking advantage of first-order reflected (echo) signals to perform RPE in order to detect the ranges and velocities of objects (targets) in its surroundings, while the UE performs JCDE as illustrated in Figure 4. As depicted in the figure, it is assumed that a total of PBP_{\mathrm{B}} target-originated echo signals reach the BS, which might be either from UE or other objects in the ambient. In turn, each UE is assumed to receive the signal transmitted by the BS scattered onto PU+1P_{\mathrm{U}}+1 paths, with pU=0p_{\mathrm{U}}=0 denoting the line-of-sight (LoS), without loss of generality (wlg), and the remaining PU≤PBP_{\mathrm{U}}\leq P_{\mathrm{B}} paths being non-LoS (NLoS) components of the multi-path channel.

For the sake of simplicity and again wlg, we shall hereafter attain to a single user, since the multi-user (MU) case has no impact onto the JCDE procedure performed independently at each user, and is transparent to the RPE algorithm, as long as the radar receiver has sufficient degrees-of-freedom (DoF) to resolve all PBP_{\mathrm{B}} echoed signals it receives. Also for simplicity, although we differentiate PBP_{\mathrm{B}} and PUP_{\mathrm{U}} in Figure 4, in the equations that follow, the number of paths/targets will be denoted by PP, with the distinction between the two cases left to context.

Finally, for the sake of enabling direct comparison with legacy (OFDM) and SotA (OTFS) approaches, it shall be assumed that the BS is capable of performing perfect SIC 55 5 The problem of SIC mitigation for the purpose of RPE in AFDM has already been addressed in [23], and solutions for the related problems of interference cancellation in orthogonal chirp division multiplexing (OCDM), or more generally for in-band interference cancellation in single antenna systems have also been proposed e.g.e.g. in [36] and [37], respectively, which support the feasibility of the assumption. prior to RPE, to the advantage of the OFDM and OTFS approaches, since it has been shown [23] that SIC is more challenging and has higher computational complexity under those waveforms than under AFDM.

II-A Generalized Doubly-Dispersive Channel Model

Consider a general doubly-dispersive wireless channel model [16] characterized by 11 LoS and PP NLoS propagation paths, with each pp-th path comprising an uncorrelated complex fading gain hp∈ℂh_{p}\in\mathbb{C}, a path delay τp∈[0,τmax]\tau_{p}\in[0,\tau_{\text{max}}] and a Doppler shift νp∈[−νmax,νmax]\nu_{p}\in[-\nu_{\text{max}},\nu_{\text{max}}], respectively. The delays and Doppler shifts of the doubly-dispersive channel are assumed to be bounded by a maximum delay τmax\tau_{\text{max}}[s] and a maximum Doppler shift νmax\nu_{\text{max}}[Hz], respectively, such that the time domain (TD) channel impulse response can be described by [38]

h⁡(t,τ)≜∑p=0Php⋅ej​2​π​νp​t⋅δ⁡(τ−τp),h(t,\tau)\triangleq\sum_{p=0}^{P}h_{p}\cdot e^{j2\pi\nu_{p}t}\cdot\delta(\tau-\tau_{p}), (1)

where tt and τ\tau are the continuous time and delays, respectively.

Leveraging equation (1), the input-output relationship of the channel in the TD can be obtained via the linear convolution of the transmit signal s⁡(t)s(t) and channel impulse response as described in [38, eq. (10.69)], which added with noise yields

r⁡(t)=s⁡(t)∗h⁡(t,τ)+w⁡(t)\displaystyle r(t)=s(t)*h(t,\tau)+w(t) (2)
≜∫−∞+∞s⁡(t−τ)​(∑p=0Php⋅ej​2​π​νp​t⋅δ⁡(τ−τp))​𝑑τ+w⁡(t),\displaystyle\hskip-117.5413pt\triangleq\int\limits_{-\infty}^{+\infty}s(t-\tau)\bigg(\sum_{p=0}^{P}h_{p}\cdot e^{j2\pi\nu_{p}t}\cdot\delta(\tau-\tau_{p})\bigg)d\tau+w(t),

where r⁡(t)r(t) and w⁡(t)w(t) are the received signal and additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN), respectively.

Defining r⁡[n]r[n] and s⁡[n]s[n], with n∈{0,…,N−1}n\in\{0,\dots,N-1\}, to be the sampled sequences of r⁡(t)r(t) and s⁡(t)s(t), respectively, with samples taken at a sufficiently high sampling rate fS≜1TSf_{\mathrm{S}}\triangleq\frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{S}}}[Hz], the following discrete equivalent of equation (2) can be obtained

r⁡[n]=∑ℓ=0∞s⁡[n−ℓ]​(∑p=0Php⋅ej​2​π​νpfS​n⋅δ⁡(ℓ−τpTS))+w⁡[n],r[n]=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}s[n-\ell]\bigg(\sum_{p=0}^{P}h_{p}\cdot e^{j2\pi\frac{\nu_{p}}{f_{\mathrm{S}}}n}\cdot\delta\Big(\ell-\frac{\tau_{p}}{T_{\mathrm{S}}}\Big)\bigg)+w[n],\vskip-4.30554pt (3)

where ℓ\ell is the normalized discrete delay index, and TST_{\mathrm{S}} the delay resolution as well as the sampling interval, such that τ=ℓ⋅TS\tau=\ell\cdot T_{\mathrm{S}}.

𝐫=(∑p=0Php⋅𝚽p⋅𝛀fp⋅𝚷ℓp)⋅𝐬+𝐰=𝐇⋅𝐬+𝐰,\mathbf{r}=\bigg(\sum_{p=0}^{P}h_{p}\cdot\mathbf{\Phi}_{p}\cdot\bm{\Omega}^{f_{p}}\cdot\mathbf{\Pi}^{\ell_{p}}\bigg)\cdot\mathbf{s}+\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{H}\cdot\mathbf{s}+\mathbf{w},\vskip-4.30554pt (4)

where the inclusion and posterior removal of a cyclic prefix (CP) of length NCPN_{\text{CP}} to the sequence s⁡[n]s[n] is already taken into account [16].

In equation (4), 𝐫≜[r⁡[0],⋯,r⁡[N−1]]∈ℂN×1\mathbf{r}\triangleq[r[0],\cdots,r[N-1]]\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times 1} and 𝐬≜[s⁡[0],⋯,s⁡[N−1]]∈ℂN×1\mathbf{s}\triangleq[s[0],\cdots,s[N-1]]\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times 1} are the transmit and received signal sample vectors; 𝐰∈ℂN×1\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times 1} denotes AWGN; 𝐇∈ℂN×N\mathbf{H}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times N} is the effective channel matrix; 𝚽p∈ℂN×N\mathbf{\Phi}_{p}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times N} described in equation (5) is a diagonal matrix which captures the effect of the CP onto the pp-th channel path, where ϕCP​(n)\phi_{\mathrm{CP}}(n) denotes a phase function on the sample index n∈{0,⋯,N−1}n\in\{0,\cdots,N-1\} [16] depending on the specific waveform used; 𝛀∈ℂN×N\bm{\Omega}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times N}, described in equation (6), is a diagonal matrix containing the NN complex roots of one and 𝚷∈{0,1}N×N\mathbf{\Pi}\in\{0,1\}^{N\times N} is the forward cyclic shift matrix66 6 To clarify, the matrix 𝚷\mathbf{\Pi} is such that 𝑨⋅𝚷ℓp\bm{A}\cdot\mathbf{\Pi}^{\ell_{p}}, with ℓp∈ℕ0\ell_{p}\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, is a cyclic left-shifted version of the matrix 𝑨\bm{A}, such that the first ℓp\ell_{p} columns of 𝑨\bm{A} are moved to the positions of the last ℓp\ell_{p} columns. Notice also that 𝚷0\mathbf{\Pi}^{0} is the N×NN\times N identity matrix, such that 𝑨⋅𝚷0=𝑨\bm{A}\cdot\mathbf{\Pi}^{0}=\bm{A}., with elements given by

πi,j=δi,j+1+δi,j−(N−1)​where​δi​j≜{0if ​i≠j,1if ​i=j.\pi_{i,j}=\delta_{i,j+1}+\delta_{i,j-(N-1)}\;\;\text{where}\;\;\delta_{ij}\triangleq\begin{cases}0&\text{if }i\neq j,\\ 1&\text{if }i=j.\end{cases}\vskip-1.07639pt (7)

Notice that the channel 𝐇\mathbf{H} implicitly defined in (4) is a general representation of a doubly-dispersive channel [38], which shall be exploited in the sequel to formulate estimation and detection models over various waveforms.

To that end, we consider the OFDM, OTFS and AFDM waveforms, which are known to perform well in doubly-dispersive channels. Since a thorough comparison of the different individual features of each of them has been done in [16], we limit ourselves here to briefly revise the models introduced thereby with the objective of obtaining a general mathematical formulation for the design of receivers/estimators for these waveforms under a common framework.

II-B OFDM Signal Model

Let 𝒞∈ℂQ×1\mathcal{C}\in\mathbb{C}^{Q\times 1} denote an arbitrary complex constellation of cardinality QQ and average energy ESE_{\mathrm{S}}, associated with a given digital modulation scheme. In OFDM, an input information vector 𝐱∈𝒞N×1\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{C}^{N\times 1} containing NN symbols taken from 𝒞\mathcal{C} are modulated into the transmit signal

𝐬OFDM=𝐅N𝖧⋅𝐱∈ℂN×1,\mathbf{s}_{\text{OFDM}}=\mathbf{F}_{N}^{\mathsf{H}}\cdot\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times 1}, (8)

where 𝐅N\mathbf{F}_{N} denotes the NN-point normalized discrete Fourier transform (DFT) matrix.

After undergoing the circular convolution with the doubly-dispersive channel, the corresponding OFDM receive signal can be written in a form similar to that of equation (4), namely

𝐫OFDM≜𝐇⋅𝐬OFDM+𝐰∈ℂN×1,\mathbf{r}_{\text{OFDM}}\triangleq\mathbf{H}\cdot\mathbf{s}_{\text{OFDM}}+\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times 1},\vskip-2.15277pt (9)

which can be demodulated into

𝐲OFDM=𝐅N⋅𝐫OFDM∈ℂN×1.\mathbf{y}_{\text{OFDM}}=\mathbf{F}_{N}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{\text{OFDM}}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times 1}.\vskip-2.15277pt (10)

From equations (9) and (10), one obtains a straightforward input-output relationship for OFDM modulation, namely

𝐲OFDM=𝐆OFDM⋅𝐱+𝐰~∈ℂN×1,\mathbf{y}_{\text{OFDM}}=\mathbf{G}_{\text{OFDM}}\cdot\mathbf{x}+\tilde{\mathbf{w}}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times 1},\vskip-2.15277pt (11)

where 𝐰~≜𝐅N​𝐰∈ℂN×1\tilde{\mathbf{w}}\triangleq\mathbf{F}_{N}\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times 1} is an equivalent AWGN vector with the same statistics as 𝐰\mathbf{w}, while 𝐆OFDM\mathbf{G}_{\text{OFDM}} is the effective OFDM channel, defined by

𝐆OFDM≜∑p=0Php⋅𝐅N⋅(𝛀fp⋅𝚷ℓp)⋅𝐅N𝖧,\mathbf{G}_{\text{OFDM}}\triangleq\sum_{p=0}^{P}h_{p}\cdot\mathbf{F}_{N}\cdot(\bm{\Omega}^{f_{p}}\cdot\mathbf{\Pi}^{\ell_{p}})\cdot\mathbf{F}_{N}^{\mathsf{H}}, (12)

with the CP phase matrices 𝚽p\mathbf{\Phi}_{p} appearing in equation (4) reduced to identity matrices [16]; i.e.,i.e., ϕCP​(n)=0\phi_{\mathrm{CP}}(n)=0 in equation (5) since there is no phase offset in the CP of OFDM signals.

II-C OTFS Signal Model

Consider an OTFS system in which an input information matrix 𝐗∈𝒞K×M\mathbf{X}\in\mathcal{C}^{K\times M}, containing K×MK\times M complex symbols taken from an arbitrary constellation 𝒞\mathcal{C}, is modulated into the transmit signal77 7 For simplicity, we assume that all pulse-shaping operations utilize rectangular waveforms, such that the corresponding sample matrices can be reduced to identity matrices.

𝐬OTFS≜vec​(𝐒)=(𝐅M𝖧⊗𝐈K)⋅𝐱∈ℂK​M×1,\mathbf{s}_{\text{OTFS}}\triangleq\text{vec}(\mathbf{S})=(\mathbf{F}_{M}^{\mathsf{H}}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{K})\cdot\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{C}^{KM\times 1}, (13)

where vec​(⋅)\text{vec}(\cdot) denotes the vectorization of a matrix, obtained by stacking the columns; the symbol ⊗\otimes denotes Kronecker product; and 𝐒\mathbf{S} is a TD symbol matrix obtained88 8 Equivalently, 𝐒\mathbf{S} can be obtained as the Heisenberg transform of the inverse symplectic finite Fourier transform (ISFFT) of 𝐗\mathbf{X}, i.e.i.e. 𝐒=𝐅K𝖧​𝐗FT\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{F}_{K}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathbf{X}_{\text{FT}} with 𝐗FT≜𝐅K​𝐗𝐅M𝖧∈ℂK×M\mathbf{X}_{\text{FT}}\triangleq\mathbf{F}_{K}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{F}_{M}^{\mathsf{H}}\in\mathbb{C}^{K\times M}. from the inverse discrete Zak transform (IDZT) of 𝐗\mathbf{X}, i.e.i.e. [18]

𝐒=𝐗𝐅M𝖧∈ℂK×M.\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{F}_{M}^{\mathsf{H}}\in\mathbb{C}^{K\times M}. (14)

We highlight that the notation in equation (13) is in line with the strategy described e.g.e.g. in [39], whereby the OTFS signals are first vectorized and then appended with a CP of length NC​PN_{CP} in order to eliminate inter-frame interference, in similarity with OFDM. Taking advantage of such similarity, and in order to allow for direct comparisons between the two waveforms, we shall hereafter set K×M=NK\times M=N.

After transmission over the doubly-dispersive channel 𝐇\mathbf{H}, the OTFS receive signal can be modeled as

𝐫OTFS≜𝐇⋅𝐬OTFS+𝐰∈ℂN×1,\mathbf{r}_{\text{OTFS}}\triangleq\mathbf{H}\cdot\mathbf{s}_{\text{OTFS}}+\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times 1}, (15)

which is analogous to the OFDM model of equation (11).

Unlike OFDM, however, the detection of the information symbols in 𝐱\mathbf{x} from 𝐫OTFS\mathbf{r}_{\text{OTFS}} requires reversing the vectorization and the IDZT operations employed in the construction of 𝐬OTFS\mathbf{s}_{\text{OTFS}}, resulting in a distinct effective channel.

In particular, let 𝐑≜vec−1​(𝐫OTFS)∈ℂK×M\mathbf{R}\triangleq\text{vec}^{-1}(\mathbf{r}_{\text{OTFS}})\in\mathbb{C}^{K\times M}, where vec−1​(⋅)\text{vec}^{-1}(\cdot) denotes the de-vectorization operation whereby a vector of size K​M×1KM\times 1 is reshaped into a matrix of size K×MK\times M, and consider the corresponding discrete Zak transform (DZT) 99 9 Equivalently, 𝐘\mathbf{Y} can be obtained as the symplectic finite Fourier transform (SFFT) of the Wigner transform 𝐘FT≜𝐅K​𝐑\mathbf{Y}_{\text{FT}}\triangleq\mathbf{F}_{K}\mathbf{R} of the matrix 𝐑\mathbf{R}, which yields 𝐘=𝐅K𝖧​𝐘FT​𝐅M∈ℂK×M\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{F}_{K}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathbf{Y}_{\text{FT}}\mathbf{F}_{M}\in\mathbb{C}^{K\times M}.

𝐘=𝐑𝐅M∈ℂK×M.\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{R}\mathbf{F}_{M}\in\mathbb{C}^{K\times M}. (16)

The corresponding demodulated OTFS signal is given by

𝐲OTFS≜vec​(𝐘)=(𝐅M⊗𝐈K)⋅𝐫OTFS∈ℂN×1,\mathbf{y}_{\text{OTFS}}\triangleq\text{vec}(\mathbf{Y})=(\mathbf{F}_{M}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{K})\cdot\mathbf{r}_{\text{OTFS}}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times 1}, (17)

which in turn can be rewritten in the form of the direct input-output relation

𝐲OTFS=𝐆OTFS⋅𝐱+𝐰~OTFS∈ℂN×1,\mathbf{y}_{\text{OTFS}}=\mathbf{G}_{\text{OTFS}}\cdot\mathbf{x}+\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{\text{OTFS}}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times 1}, (18)

where 𝐰~OTFS≜(𝐅M⊗𝐈K)⋅𝐰∈ℂN×1\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{\text{OTFS}}\triangleq(\mathbf{F}_{M}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{K})\cdot\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times 1} is an equivalent AWGN vector with the same statistics as 𝐰\mathbf{w}, while 𝐆OTFS∈ℂN×N\mathbf{G}_{\text{OTFS}}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times N} is the effective OTFS channel in the DD domain, defined by

𝐆OTFS≜∑p=0Php⋅(𝐅M⊗𝐈K)⋅(𝛀fp⋅𝚷ℓp)⋅(𝐅M𝖧⊗𝐈K),\mathbf{G}_{\text{OTFS}}\triangleq\sum_{p=0}^{P}h_{p}\cdot(\mathbf{F}_{M}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{K})\cdot(\bm{\Omega}^{f_{p}}\cdot\mathbf{\Pi}^{\ell_{p}})\cdot(\mathbf{F}_{M}^{\mathsf{H}}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{K}), (19)

in which, similar to the OFDM waveform, the CP phase matrices 𝚽p\mathbf{\Phi}_{p} have been reduced to identity matrices [16].

Comparing equations (12) and (19), one can appreciate how the channel modeling approach of [16] elucidates both the similarity in form, and the distinction in effect between the OFDM and OTFS waveforms in doubly-dispersive channels.

II-D AFDM Signal Model

Finally, let us describe the input-output relationship of the AFDM waveform associated with a doubly-dispersive channel. Similarly to the above, letting 𝐱\mathbf{x} denote the information vector with symbols taken from the constellation 𝒞\mathcal{C}, the corresponding AFDM modulated transmit signal is given by its inverse discrete affine Fourier transform (IDAFT), i.e.i.e.

𝐬AFDM=(𝚲1𝖧​𝐅N𝖧​𝚲2𝖧)⋅𝐱∈ℂN×1,\mathbf{s}_{\text{AFDM}}=(\mathbf{\Lambda}_{1}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathbf{F}_{N}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathbf{\Lambda}_{2}^{\mathsf{H}})\cdot\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times 1}, (20)

with the matrices 𝚲i\mathbf{\Lambda}_{i} defined as

𝚲i≜diag​([1,⋯,e−j​2​π​ci​n2,⋯,e−j​2​π​ci​(N−1)2])∈ℂN×N,\mathbf{\Lambda}_{i}\triangleq\text{diag}\big(\big[1,\cdots,e^{-j2\pi c_{i}n^{2}},\cdots,e^{-j2\pi c_{i}(N-1)^{2}}\big]\big)\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times N}, (21)

where the constants c1c_{1} and c2c_{2} are chosen appropriately to match the maximum Doppler of the channel, and include the insertion of a chirp-periodic prefix (CPP) to mitigate the effects of multipath propagation [22].

It was shown in [16] that after going through a doubly-dispersive channel, an AFDM modulated symbol vector as given in equation (20) with the inclusion of a CPP as described in [22], can be modeled similarly to equation (4), only with the CP matrix 𝚽p\bm{\Phi}_{p} of equation (5) replaced by the corresponding CPP matrix 𝚽p\bm{\varPhi}_{p} as explicitly given in equation (22) (i.e.,i.e., ϕCP​(n)=c1​(N2−2​N​n)\phi_{\mathrm{CP}}(n)=c_{1}(N^{2}-2Nn) in equation (5)), such that the corresponding received signal is given by

𝐫AFDM≜𝐇⋅𝐬AFDM+𝐰∈ℂN×1.\mathbf{r}_{\text{AFDM}}\triangleq\mathbf{H}\cdot\mathbf{s}_{\text{AFDM}}+\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times 1}. (23)

Demodulating the signal in equation (23) yields

𝐲AFDM=(𝚲2​𝐅N​𝚲1)⋅𝐫AFDM∈ℂN×1,\mathbf{y}_{\text{AFDM}}=(\mathbf{\Lambda}_{2}\mathbf{F}_{N}\mathbf{\Lambda}_{1})\cdot\mathbf{r}_{\text{AFDM}}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times 1}, (24)

which in turn can be expressed as

𝐲AFDM=𝐆AFDM⋅𝐱+𝐰~AFDM∈ℂN×1,\mathbf{y}_{\text{AFDM}}=\mathbf{G}_{\text{AFDM}}\cdot\mathbf{x}+\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{\text{AFDM}}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times 1}, (25)

where 𝐰~AFDM≜(𝚲2​𝐅N​𝚲1)⋅𝐰∈ℂN×1\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{\text{AFDM}}\triangleq(\mathbf{\Lambda}_{2}\mathbf{F}_{N}\mathbf{\Lambda}_{1})\cdot\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times 1} is an equivalent AWGN vector with the same statistics as 𝐰\mathbf{w}, and 𝐆AFDM∈ℂN×N\mathbf{G}_{\text{AFDM}}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times N} in the effective AFDM channel matrix, given by

𝐆AFDM≜∑p=0Php⋅(𝚲2​𝐅N​𝚲1)⋅(𝚽p⋅𝛀fp⋅𝚷ℓp)⋅(𝚲1𝖧​𝐅N𝖧​𝚲2𝖧),\mathbf{G}_{\text{AFDM}}\triangleq\sum_{p=0}^{P}h_{p}\cdot(\mathbf{\Lambda}_{2}\mathbf{F}_{N}\mathbf{\Lambda}_{1})\cdot(\bm{\varPhi}_{p}\cdot\bm{\Omega}^{f_{p}}\cdot\mathbf{\Pi}^{\ell_{p}})\cdot(\mathbf{\Lambda}_{1}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathbf{F}_{N}^{\mathsf{H}}\mathbf{\Lambda}_{2}^{\mathsf{H}}), (26)

where we emphasize that 𝚽p\bm{\varPhi}_{p} is as in equation (22).

Once again, it is clear that equations (12), (19) and (26) have the same structure, as do the input-output relationships described by equations (11), (18) and (25), such that the JCDE and RPE techniques proposed in the sequel are applicable to OFDM, OTFS and AFDM waveforms alike.

III Joint Channel and Data Estimation

In this section, we introduce the proposed JCDE method for OFDM, OTFS and AFDM systems, under the general system model described in the previous section, and compare their relative performances. For the sake of convenience, we shall express the effective channels for the three waveforms given in equations (12), (19) and (26) in the form

𝐲=∑p=0Php⋅𝚪p⋅𝐱+𝐰~∈ℂN×1,\mathbf{y}=\sum_{p=0}^{P}h_{p}\cdot\mathbf{\Gamma}_{p}\cdot\mathbf{x}+\tilde{\mathbf{w}}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times 1}, (27)

where the matrices 𝚪p\mathbf{\Gamma}_{p} captures the long-term delay-Doppler statistics of the channel, which are assumed to be known1010 10 According to [40, 41, 42], the delay and Doppler shifts can be assumed constant during multiple frame transmissions, enabling sporadic estimation of 𝚪p,∀p\mathbf{\Gamma}_{p},\forall p via RPE schemes utilizing pilots such as the method described in the latter part of Section IV-B. However, the addition of this procedure into the JCDE scheme transforms this into an RPE-aided JCDE method (i.e.,i.e., user-centric RPE) which while consolidating and combining the seperate aspects of ISAC, deserves further attention and will be addressed in a follow-up article..

From equation (27), it is evident that each received signal in 𝐲\mathbf{y} can be described by

yn=∑p=0P∑m=0N−1hp⋅γp:n,m⋅xm+w~n,y_{n}=\sum_{p=0}^{P}\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}h_{p}\cdot\gamma_{p:n,m}\cdot x_{m}+\tilde{w}_{n}, (28)

where we slightly deviate from the notation employed earlier in equation (3) by denoting the mm-th information symbol as xmx_{m} instead of x⁡[m]x[m], and accordingly the nn-th receive signal sample by yny_{n} instead of y⁡[n]y[n], for future convenience.

III-A JCDE via Parametric Bilinear Gaussian Belief Propagation

We have first proposed the PBiGaBP framework for JCDE under OTFS signaling in [1]. Thanks to the generalized channel model described above, however, it is obvious that the same technique applies to OFDM and AFDM as well. We therefore proceed to succinctly describe the approach, referring the reader to [1] for further details.

For starters, referring to Figure 2, it is initially assumed1111 11 Later we shall adopt the strategy proposed in [22] and consider, for the AFDM case, the alternative of utilizing only one pilot followed by a null-guard interval of length B−1B-1 among the NN symbols in 𝐱\mathbf{x}, for the purpose of enabling the RPE scheme of Section IV-B. that in any of the three systems compared, a block of BB pilots1212 12 We use the first column of the B×BB\times B Zadoff-Chu sequence [1] as our pilot column. is embedded in the N×1N\times 1 symbol vector 𝐱\mathbf{x}.

We shall also clarify that although the placement of pilots amidst payload (data) symbols can be optimized under various criteria [43], in the context of our discussion where issues such as distortions due hardware imperfection [44], pilot contamination [45], and channel aging [28] are not considered, the location of pilots has no effect on the performance of the JCDE. Suffice it therefore, to consider the amount of power allocated to pilots, relative to that allocated to data symbols.

With these issues addressed, the PBiGaBP framework for JCDE introduced here can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    Soft interference cancellation (soft IC), which consists of removing the inter-symbol interference from 𝐲\mathbf{y}, by using temporary estimates (soft replicas) of 𝐡\mathbf{h} and 𝐱\mathbf{x} generated in the previous iteration;

  • •

    Belief generation (BG), whereby the likelihood (beliefs) of the estimates of 𝐡\mathbf{h} and 𝐱\mathbf{x} are obtained from 𝐲\mathbf{y} after soft IC and under scalar Gaussian approximation (SGA);

  • •

    Soft replica generation (soft RG), whereby soft replicas are generated from the beliefs via conditional expectations.

The signal processing operations corresponding to each of these steps are described below.

III-A1 Soft IC

Let us consider the ii-th iteration of the algorithm, and denote the soft replicas of the mm-th symbol and the pp-th channel gain associated with the nn-th receive signal yny_{n}, at the previous iteration respectively by x^n,m(i−1)\hat{x}_{n,m}^{(i-1)} and h^n,p(i−1)\hat{h}_{n,p}^{(i-1)}. Then, the mean-squared-errors (MSEs) of these estimates computed for the ii-th iteration are given by

σ^x:n,m2​(i)≜𝔼x[|x−x^n,m(i−1)|2]=ES−|x^n,m(i−1)|2,∀(n,m),\hat{\sigma}^{2(i)}_{x:{n,m}}\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{x}\big[|x-\hat{x}_{n,m}^{(i-1)}|^{2}\big]=E_{\mathrm{S}}-|\hat{x}_{n,m}^{(i-1)}|^{2},\forall(n,m), (29a)
σ^h:n,p2​(i)≜𝔼h[|h−h^n,p(i−1)|2]=σh2−|h^n,p(i−1)|2,∀(n,p),\hat{\sigma}^{2(i)}_{h:{n,p}}\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{h}\big[|h-\hat{h}_{n,p}^{(i-1)}|^{2}\big]=\sigma_{h}^{2}-|\hat{h}_{n,p}^{(i-1)}|^{2},\forall(n,p), (29b)
where 𝔼x\mathbb{E}_{x} refers to expectation over the all possible symbols xx in the constellation 𝒞\mathcal{C}, while 𝔼h\mathbb{E}_{h} refers to expectation over all possible outcomes of h∼𝒞​𝒩​(0,σh2)h\sim\mathcal{CN}(0,\sigma^{2}_{h}), respectively1313 13 Although the average power of each channel path may be generally different, especially in sub-6GHz channels where the propagation lengths of different paths can vary from meters to kilometers, it is commonly assumed in high-frequency (mmWave and TeraHz) channels, where ranges are much shorter, that the gains of all paths follow the same distribution [21, 22, 23]..

At a given ii-th iteration, the objective of the soft IC step is to compute the symbol- and channel-centric replicas y~x:m,n(i)\tilde{y}_{x:{m,n}}^{(i)} and y~h:p,n(i)\tilde{y}_{h:{p,n}}^{(i)} and the corresponding variances σ~2​(i)x:m,n\tilde{\sigma}^{2(i)}_{x:{m,n}} and σ~2​(i)h:p,n\tilde{\sigma}^{2(i)}_{h:{p,n}}, using the soft estimates x^n,m(i−1)\hat{x}_{n,m}^{(i-1)} and h^n,p(i−1)\hat{h}_{n,p}^{(i-1)} and their variances σ^x:n,m2​(i−1)\hat{\sigma}_{x:{n,m}}^{2(i-1)} and σ^2​(i−1)h:n,p\hat{\sigma}^{2(i-1)}_{h:{n,p}} obtained in the previous iteration.

In view of equation (28), we straightforwardly have

y~x:m,n(i)=yn−∑p=0P∑q≠mN−1h^n,p(i−1)⋅γp:n,q⋅x^n,q(i−1).\tilde{y}_{x:{m,n}}^{(i)}=y_{n}-\sum_{p=0}^{P}\sum_{q\neq m}^{N-1}\hat{h}_{n,p}^{(i-1)}\cdot\gamma_{p:n,q}\cdot\hat{x}_{n,q}^{(i-1)}. (30)

These soft IC receive signal replicas follow Gaussian probability density functions (PDFs), namely

y~x:m,n(i)∼pyn|xm(yn|xm)∝exp(−|yn−γ~x:m,n(i)xm|2σ~2​(i)x:m,n),\tilde{y}_{x:{m,n}}^{(i)}\sim p_{\text{y}_{n}|x_{m}}(\text{y}_{n}|x_{m})\propto\text{exp}\bigg(\!-\frac{|\text{y}_{n}\!-\!\tilde{\gamma}_{x:{m,n}}^{(i)}x_{m}|^{2}}{\tilde{\sigma}^{2(i)}_{x:{m,n}}}\bigg), (31)

where yn\text{y}_{n} is an auxiliary variable and γ~x:m,n(i)\tilde{\gamma}_{x:{m,n}}^{(i)} are the corresponding soft IC effective channel gains, defined as

γ~x:m,n(i)≜∑p=0Ph^n,p(i−1)γp:n,m,\tilde{\gamma}_{x:{m,n}}^{(i)}\triangleq\sum_{p=0}^{P}\hat{h}_{n,p}^{(i-1)}\gamma_{p:n,m}, (32)

while σ~2​(i)x:m,n\tilde{\sigma}^{2(i)}_{x:{m,n}} are the soft IC conditional variances approximated by replacing the instantaneous values with the long-term statistics [46, 47] as

σ~x:m,n2​(i)≜𝔼x,h[|y~x:m,n(i)−γ~x:m,n(i)xm|2]\displaystyle\hskip-2.15277pt\tilde{\sigma}^{2(i)}_{x:{m,n}}\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{{x},h}\big[|\tilde{y}_{x:{m,n}}^{(i)}-\tilde{\gamma}_{x:{m,n}}^{(i)}x_{m}|^{2}\big] (33)
≈∑p=0Pσ^2​(i−1)h:n,p|y^(i)xm:n,p|2+∑q≠mN−1σ^x:n,q2​(i−1)|γ~x:q,n(i)|2+N0+\displaystyle\hskip-169.63832pt\approx\sum_{p=0}^{P}\hat{\sigma}^{2(i-1)}_{h:{n,p}}|\hat{y}^{(i)}_{x_{m}:n,p}|^{2}+\sum_{q\neq m}^{N-1}\hat{\sigma}_{x:{n,q}}^{2(i-1)}|\tilde{\gamma}_{x:q,n}^{(i)}|^{2}+N_{0}+
∑p=0Pσ^2​(i−1)h:n,p∑q≠mN−1σ^x:n,q2​(i−1)|γp:n,q|2+ES∑p=0Pσ^2​(i−1)h:n,p|γp:n,m|2,\displaystyle\hskip-159.30505pt\sum_{p=0}^{P}\hat{\sigma}^{2(i-1)}_{h:{n,p}}\sum_{q\neq m}^{N-1}\hat{\sigma}_{x:{n,q}}^{2(i-1)}|\gamma_{p:n,q}|^{2}\!+\!E_{\mathrm{S}}\sum_{p=0}^{P}\hat{\sigma}^{2(i-1)}_{h:{n,p}}|\gamma_{p:n,m}|^{2},

with y^(i)xm:n,p\hat{y}^{(i)}_{x_{m}:n,p} denoting the received signal estimate after cancellation of the mm-th soft symbol estimate, which is given by

y^(i)xm:n,p≜∑q≠mN−1γp:n,qx^n,q(i−1).\hat{y}^{(i)}_{x_{m}:n,p}\triangleq\sum_{q\neq m}^{N-1}\gamma_{p:n,q}\hat{x}_{n,q}^{(i-1)}. (34)

Similarly, the channel-centric replica can be computed as

y~h:p,n(i)=yn−∑q≠pPh^n,q(i)⋅y^h:n,q(i),\tilde{y}_{h:{p,n}}^{(i)}=y_{n}-\sum_{q\neq p}^{P}\hat{h}_{n,q}^{(i)}\cdot\hat{y}_{h:{n,q}}^{(i)}, (35)

with the corresponding variance given by

σ~2​(i)h:p,n≜∑q≠pPσ^h:n,q2​(i−1)|y^h:n,q(i)|2+∑m=0N−1σ^2​(i−1)x:n,m|γ~hp:m,n(i)|2+N0+\displaystyle\tilde{\sigma}^{2(i)}_{h:{p,n}}\!\triangleq\!\sum_{q\neq p}^{P}\!\hat{\sigma}_{h:{n,q}}^{2(i-1)}|\hat{y}_{h:{n,q}}^{(i)}|^{2}\!+\!\!\!\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}\!\!\hat{\sigma}^{2(i-1)}_{x:{n,m}}|\tilde{\gamma}_{h_{p}:{m,n}}^{(i)}|^{2}\!+\!N_{0}+\!\! (36)
∑q≠pPσ^h:n,q2​(i)∑m=0N−1σ^2​(i)x:n,m|γq,n​m|2+σ2h∑m=0N−1σ^2​(i)x:n,m|γp:n,m|2,\displaystyle\hskip-206.66602pt\sum_{q\neq p}^{P}\!\!\hat{\sigma}_{h:{n,q}}^{2(i)}\!\!\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}\!\!\hat{\sigma}^{2(i)}_{x:{n,m}}|\gamma_{q,nm}|^{2}\!+\!\sigma^{2}_{h}\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}\hat{\sigma}^{2(i)}_{x:{n,m}}|\gamma_{p:n,m}|^{2}\!,

where y^h:n,p(i)\hat{y}_{h:{n,p}}^{(i)} is the channel-centric soft channel estimate and γ~hp:m,n(i)\tilde{\gamma}_{h_{p}:{m,n}}^{(i)} is the corresponding soft IC effective channel gain of the pp-th path, respectively given by

y^h:n,p(i)≜∑m=0N−1γp:n,mx^n,m(i−1)andγ~hp:m,n(i)≜∑q≠pPh^n,q(i−1)γq,n​m.\hat{y}_{h:{n,p}}^{(i)}\triangleq\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}\gamma_{p:n,m}\hat{x}_{n,m}^{(i-1)}\;\,\text{and}\;\,\tilde{\gamma}_{h_{p}:{m,n}}^{(i)}\triangleq\sum_{q\neq p}^{P}\hat{h}_{n,q}^{(i-1)}\gamma_{q,nm}. (37)

III-A2 Belief Generation

In order to generate the beliefs of all symbols, consider the effect of substituting equation (28) into (30) such that the SGA holds under the assumption that N×PN\times P is a sufficiently large number, and that the individual estimation errors in h^n,p(i−1)\hat{h}_{n,p}^{(i-1)} and x^n,q(i−1)\hat{x}_{n,q}^{(i-1)} are independent.

Then, as a result of SGA, the belief corresponding to the mm-th symbol xmx_{m} at the nn-th factor node is obtained by combining the contributions of all signals in 𝐲\mathbf{y}, excluding yny_{n}, under the PDF

px|xm(x|xm)=∏q≠nNpyq|xm(yq|xm)∝exp(−|x−x~n,m(i)|2σ~x~:n,m2​(i)),\!\!\!\!p_{\text{x}|x_{m}}(\text{x}|x_{m})\!=\!\prod_{q\neq n}^{N}\!p_{\text{y}_{q}|\text{x}_{m}}(\text{y}_{q}|x_{m})\propto\text{exp}\bigg(\!\!\!-\!\frac{|\text{x}\!-\!\tilde{x}_{n,m}^{(i)}|^{2}}{\tilde{\sigma}_{\tilde{x}:{n,m}}^{2(i)}}\!\bigg),\! (38)

such that the desired beliefs and their variances are given by

x~n,m(i)≜σ~x~:n,m2​(i)∑q≠nNγ~x:m,q∗(i)y~x:m,q(i)σ~x:m,q2​(i)andσ~x~:n,m2​(i)≜(∑q≠nN|γ~x:m,q(i)|2σ~x:m,q2​(i))−1.\tilde{x}_{n,m}^{(i)}\!\!\triangleq\!\tilde{\sigma}_{\tilde{x}:{n,m}}^{2(i)}\!\sum_{q\neq n}^{N}\!\!\frac{\tilde{\gamma}_{x:{m,q}}^{*(i)}\tilde{y}_{x:{m,q}}^{(i)}}{\tilde{\sigma}_{x:{m,q}}^{2(i)}}\;\,\text{and}\;\,\tilde{\sigma}_{\tilde{x}:{n,m}}^{2(i)}\!\!\triangleq\!\!\bigg(\!\sum_{q\neq n}^{N}\!\!\frac{|\tilde{\gamma}_{x:{m,q}}^{(i)}|^{2}}{\tilde{\sigma}_{x:{m,q}}^{2(i)}}\bigg)^{\!\!\!-1}\!\!\!\!. (39)

Similarly, under SGA, the extrinsic beliefs of the channel gains can be shown to follow the approximate distribution

ph|hp(h|hp)∝exp(−|h−h~n,p(i)|2σ~h~:n,p2​(i)),p_{\text{h}|h_{p}}(\text{h}|h_{p})\propto\text{exp}\bigg(-\frac{|\text{h}-\!\tilde{\;\mathrm{h}}_{n,p}^{(i)}|^{2}}{\tilde{\sigma}_{\!\tilde{\;\mathrm{h}}:{n,p}}^{2(i)}}\bigg), (40)

with corresponding beliefs and variances given by

h~n,p(i)≜σ~h~:n,p2​(i)∑q≠nNy^h:q​p∗(i)y~h:p,q(i)σ~h:p,q2​(i)andσ~h~:n,p2​(i)≜(∑q≠nN|y^h:q​p(i)|2σ~h:p,q2​(i))−1.\!\tilde{\;\mathrm{h}}_{n,p}^{(i)}\!\triangleq\!\tilde{\sigma}_{\!\tilde{\;\mathrm{h}}:{n,p}}^{2(i)}\sum_{q\neq n}^{N}\frac{\hat{y}_{h:{qp}}^{*(i)}\tilde{y}_{h:{p,q}}^{(i)}}{\tilde{\sigma}_{h:{p,q}}^{2(i)}}\;\,\text{and}\;\,\tilde{\sigma}_{\!\tilde{\;\mathrm{h}}:{n,p}}^{2(i)}\!\triangleq\!\!\bigg(\!\sum_{q\neq n}^{N}\frac{|\hat{y}_{h:{qp}}^{(i)}|^{2}}{\tilde{\sigma}_{h:{p,q}}^{2(i)}}\bigg)^{\!\!-1}\!\!\!\!\!. (41)

III-A3 Soft RG

Finally, the soft replicas of xmx_{m} and hph_{p} can be obtained from the conditional expectation given the extrinsic beliefs, again thanks to the SGA and under the assumption that the effective noise components in x^n,m(i),∀(n,m)\hat{x}_{n,m}^{(i)},\forall(n,m) and h^n,p(i),∀(n,p)\hat{h}_{n,p}^{(i)},\forall(n,p) are uncorrelated. In particular, we have

x^n,m(i)=∑x∈𝒞x⋅px|x(x|x;x~n,m(i),σ~x~:n,m2​(i))⋅px(x)∑x′∈𝒞px|x′(x|x′;x~n,m(i),σ~x~:n,m2​(i))⋅px′(x′),\hat{x}_{n,m}^{(i)}=\frac{\sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{C}}x\cdot p_{\text{x}|x}\big(\text{x}|x;\tilde{x}_{n,m}^{(i)},\tilde{\sigma}_{\tilde{x}:{n,m}}^{2(i)}\big)\cdot p_{x}(x)}{\sum\limits_{x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}}p_{\text{x}|x^{\prime}}\big(\text{x}|x^{\prime};\tilde{x}_{n,m}^{(i)},\tilde{\sigma}_{\tilde{x}:{n,m}}^{2(i)}\big)\cdot p_{x^{\prime}}(x^{\prime})}, (42)
h^n,p(i)=∫h⋅ph|h(h|h;h~n,p(i),σ~h~:n,p2​(i))⋅ph(h)∫ph|h′(h|h′;h~n,p(i),σ~h~:n,p2​(i))⋅ph′(h′),\hat{h}_{n,p}^{(i)}=\frac{\int h\cdot p_{\text{h}|h}\big(\text{h}|h;\tilde{h}_{n,p}^{(i)},\tilde{\sigma}_{\tilde{h}:{n,p}}^{2(i)}\big)\cdot p_{h}(h)}{\int p_{\text{h}|h^{\prime}}\big(\text{h}|h^{\prime};\tilde{h}_{n,p}^{(i)},\tilde{\sigma}_{\tilde{h}:{n,p}}^{2(i)}\big)\cdot p_{h^{\prime}}(h^{\prime})}, (43)

where px|x(x|x;x~n,m(i),σ~x~:n,m2​(i))p_{\text{x}|x}\big(\text{x}|x;\tilde{x}_{n,m}^{(i)},\tilde{\sigma}_{\tilde{x}:{n,m}}^{2(i)}\big) and ph|h(h|h;h~n,p(i),σ~h~:n,p2​(i))p_{\text{h}|h}\big(\text{h}|h;\tilde{h}_{n,p}^{(i)},\tilde{\sigma}_{\tilde{h}:{n,p}}^{2(i)}\big) are the likelihood functions of the data and channel beliefs given in equations (38) and (40), respectively, only with the notation extended to explicitly show the parameters (means and variances) computed above.

In order to compute the beliefs x^n,m(i)\hat{x}_{n,m}^{(i)} with basis on equation (42), suffice it to notice that under the assumption that each element xx of the data vector is independently drawn with equal probability out of the QQ-points of the constellation 𝒞\mathcal{C}, the likelihood px​(x)p_{x}(x) is a Multinomial distribution of the QQ-th order, such that for quadrature phase-shift keying (QPSK) modulation, we have

x^n,m(i)=cx⋅(tanh[2cxℜ⁡{x~n,m(i)}σ~x~:n,m2​(i)]+jtanh[2cxℑ⁡{x~n,m(i)}σ~x~:n,m2​(i)]),\hat{x}_{n,m}^{(i)}\!=\!c_{x}\!\cdot\!\bigg(\!\text{tanh}\!\bigg[2c_{x}\frac{\Re\{{\tilde{x}_{n,m}^{(i)}}\}}{\tilde{\sigma}_{\tilde{x}:{n,m}}^{2(i)}}\bigg]\!\!+\!j\text{tanh}\!\bigg[2c_{x}\frac{\Im\{{\tilde{x}_{n,m}^{(i)}}\}}{\tilde{\sigma}_{\tilde{x}:{n,m}}^{2(i)}}\bigg]\!\bigg),\!\! (44)

where cx≜ES/2c_{x}\triangleq\sqrt{E_{\mathrm{S}}/2} represents the magnitude of the real and imaginary components of the QPSK symbols.

After obtaining x^n,m(i)\hat{x}_{n,m}^{(i)} as per equation (44), the final output is computed by damping the result with a damping factor 0<βx<10<\beta_{x}<1 in order to improve convergence [48], yielding

x^n,m(i)=βx​x^n,m(i)+(1−βx)​x^n,m(i−1).\hat{x}_{n,m}^{(i)}=\beta_{x}\hat{x}_{n,m}^{(i)}+(1-\beta_{x})\hat{x}_{n,m}^{(i-1)}. (45)

In turn, the corresponding variance σ^2​(i)x:n,m\hat{\sigma}^{2(i)}_{x:{n,m}} is first updated following equation (29a), but with the updated symbol estimate, i.e.i.e., σ^2​(i)x:n,m=ES−|x^n,m(i)|2\hat{\sigma}^{2(i)}_{x:{n,m}}=E_{\mathrm{S}}-|\hat{x}_{n,m}^{(i)}|^{2}, and then damped via

σ^x:n,m2​(i)=βxσ^x:n,m2​(i)+(1−βx)σ^x:n,m2​(i−1).\hat{\sigma}^{2(i)}_{x:{n,m}}=\beta_{x}\hat{\sigma}_{x:{n,m}}^{2(i)}+(1-\beta_{x})\hat{\sigma}_{x:{n,m}}^{2(i-1)}. (46)

Similarly to the above, in order to obtain the channel estimate belief, observe that the likelihood in equation (43) is a Gaussian-product distribution, with the mean of ph​(h)p_{h}(h) equal to zero, which straightforwardly yields [49, 50]

h^n,p(i)=σh2​h~n,p(i)σ~h~:n,p2​(i)+σ2h,\hat{h}_{n,p}^{(i)}=\frac{\sigma^{2}_{h}\tilde{h}_{n,p}^{(i)}}{\tilde{\sigma}_{\tilde{h}:{n,p}}^{2(i)}+\sigma^{2}_{h}}, (47)

and

σ^2​(i)h:n,p=σ2hσ~h~:n,p2​(i)σ~h~:n,p2​(i)+σ2h,\hat{\sigma}^{2(i)}_{h:{n,p}}=\frac{\sigma^{2}_{h}\tilde{\sigma}_{\tilde{h}:{n,p}}^{2(i)}}{\tilde{\sigma}_{\tilde{h}:{n,p}}^{2(i)}+\sigma^{2}_{h}}, (48)

which are then damped with a damping factor 0<βh<10<\beta_{h}<1 as

h^n,p(i)=βh​h^n,p(i)+(1−βh)​h^n,p(i−1),\hat{h}_{n,p}^{(i)}=\beta_{h}\hat{h}_{n,p}^{(i)}+(1-\beta_{h})\hat{h}_{n,p}^{(i-1)}, (49)

and

σ^h:n,p2​(i)=βhσ^h:n,p2​(i)+(1−βh)σ^h:n,p2​(i−1).\hat{\sigma}_{h:{n,p}}^{2(i)}=\beta_{h}\hat{\sigma}_{h:{n,p}}^{2(i)}+(1-\beta_{h})\hat{\sigma}_{h:{n,p}}^{2(i-1)}. (50)

The proposed PBiGaBP-based JCDE algorithm is summarized as a pseudocode in Algorithm 1.

Remark 1: Although the proposed PBiGaBP-based JCDE algorithm is designed based on the Bayes-optimal GaBP framework, to the best of our knowledge, there exists no asymptotic analysis of the large-system limit for iterative convergence analysis of Bayesian parametric bilinear inference algorithms. While semi-analytical methods have been proposed for the prediction of the number of iterations required for fixed-point convergence in large scale systems [29, 51], they cannot be used under correlated observations. Therefore, for the performance analysis detailed in Section III-C, rigorous numerical simulations are provided to demonstrate the superiority of the proposed technique.

III-B Complexity Analysis

Since there are no high-complexity matrix inversions in the proposed PBiGaBP-based JCDE scheme detailed in Algorithm 1, the order of complexity strictly depends on the scalar operations executed. Therefore, the computational complexity of the proposed method is 𝒪​(N2​(P+1))\mathcal{O}(N^{2}(P+1)) per iteration, which is linear in terms of the operations performed, and of a much lower complexity than SotA methods based on linear minimum mean square error (LMMSE) filtering, which incur a cost of 𝒪⁡(N3)\mathcal{O}(N^{3}) due to a computation of LMMSE filter involving a matrix inversion operation.

The proposed method also has comparable complexity to the SotA parametric bilinear generalized approximate message passing (PBiGAMP) scheme given in [1], which also is of order 𝒪​(N2​(P+1))\mathcal{O}(N^{2}(P+1)), but far outperforms the latter method in terms of performance, therefore offering an excellent performance-complexity tradeoff.

III-C Performance Analysis

In this subsection, we evaluate the performance of the proposed PBiGaBP algorithm at the UE, under OFDM, OTFS and AFDM waveforms. To that end, we consider the scenario depicted in Figure 4 with 11 LoS path and 44 NLoS paths (i.e.,i.e., PU=4P_{\mathrm{U}}=4) seen at the UE; and assume a mmWave system1414 14 Although the proposed scheme can be used for arbitrary frequencies and bandwidths, our focus here is on mmWave systems due to the trend towards moving to higher frequencies in 6G and beyond [7]. operating at 70​GHz70\,\text{GHz} with a bandwidth of 20​MHz20\,\text{MHz}1515 15 With fSf_{\mathrm{S}} set to twice the bandwidth according to the Nyquist rate. and employing QPSK symbols. For the channel model, we consider a maximum normalized delay index of 2020 and a maximum normalized digital Doppler shift index of 0.250.25 (i.e., ℓmax≜τmax​fS=20\ell_{\text{max}}{\triangleq\tau_{\text{max}}f_{\mathrm{S}}}=20 and fmax≜N​νmaxfS=0.25f_{\text{max}}{\triangleq\frac{N\nu_{\text{max}}}{f_{\mathrm{S}}}}=0.25), which allows for a maximum unambiguous range of 75​m75\,\text{m} and a maximum unambiguous velocity of 602​km/h602\,\text{km/h}, respectively. This allows for the random generation of the path delays τp\tau_{p} using a uniform distribution across [0,τmax][0,\tau_{\text{max}}] and the use of Jakes Doppler spectrum [22] for the path Doppler shifts as νp=νmax​cos⁡(θp)\nu_{p}=\nu_{\text{max}}\cos(\theta_{p}), where θp\theta_{p} is uniformly distributed over [−π,π][-\pi,\pi] at each Monte Carlo iteration. As for frame parameters, we consider K=B=32K=B=32 and M=4M=4 for OTFS, and in order to sustain a fair comparison, N=128N=128 for OFDM and AFDM. Finally, regarding the PBiGaBP algorithm, we set βx,βh=0.3\beta_{x},\beta_{h}=0.3, the maximum number of iterations imax=40i_{\text{max}}=40, the constellation power ES=1E_{\mathrm{S}}=1 and the average channel power per path σh2=1\sigma_{h}^{2}=1.

First, using the Linear GaBP 1616 16 Linear GaBP is a technique that uses GaBP for both channel estimation (under full knowledge of the frame) and data decoding (under full knowledge of the channel coefficients), combined with the use of an LMMSE filtering-based initialization for channel estimation. The approach provides a lower bound on the performance for the proposed method in exchange for a large computational cost. as a baseline, we compare in Figure 3 the communications and channel estimation performances, in terms of BER and normalized mean square error (NMSE), respectively, achieved by PBiGaBP employed over OTFS, OFDM and AFDM waveforms. In this comparison, all systems employ an equal number NpN_{p} of pilot symbols, although each system has its own structure (see Section II and Figure 2).

The results show that PBiGaBP-based JCDE with AFDM and OTFS outperforms a system employing the same proposed technique but employing a legacy OFDM waveform, both in terms of BER and NMSE, with a slight advantage of AFDM over the OTFS alternative.

We highlight that a comparison between the proposed JCDE algorithm and other techniques from related literature is not offered in Figure 3, as we are unaware of any alternative JCDE solution for AFDM systems. Therefore, Figure 4 compares the proposed PBiGaBP-based JCDEboth in terms of BER and NMSE performance against the GaBP alternative to the ML-based AFDM channel estimation method from [23], where channel estimation is done solely based on the single pilot via GaBP with an accompanying GaBP-based data decoding.

We emphasize, however, that the technique in [23] is not a JCDE scheme, being rather strictly pilot-based like traditional channel estimation, such that the latter SotA method enjoys, in this comparison, the advantage of not dealing with the additional burden of performing data detection, which the proposed algorithm does. In addition, as indicated in the legend of the figure, the comparison awards the SotA approach a power advantage, by means of allowing the latter to employ pilot signals with higher power than that used in the proposed method.

The results show that the proposed PBiGaBP-based JCDE scheme outperforms the traditional pilot-only GaBP-based method for the single pilot AFDM frame structure proposed in [23] and illustrated in Figure 2 even when the latter employs a pilot with 10 times as higher power, which is a consequence of the fact that the proposed scheme takes advantage not only of the pilot, but also payload symbols (i.e.,i.e., soft pilots) to estimate the channel. The results also motivates us hereafter to no longer consider OFDM, as it is clear that this waveform is outperformed by OTFS and AFDM in doubly-dispersive channels.

IV Radar Parameter Estimation in Doubly Dispersive Channels

Having demonstrated the effectiveness of our proposed PBiGaBP-based JCDE scheme for AFDM, we next consider the radar parameter estimation problem1717 17 For the sake of simplicity, we concentrate here on the parameter estimation – as opposed to target acquisition/detection – part of the radar problem, such that the total number of targets is assumed to be known [52], and the target association problem is assumed to be solvable [53]. It is easy to perceive from the approach introduced, however, that an extension of the work here presented to joint detection and parameter estimation, such as performed in [52], is possible. That will, however, be pursued in a follow-up work., also referred to as DD domain channel estimation problem [54]. To that end, a typical DD channel [31] is hereafter assumed, characterized by a maximum normalized delay spread max​(ℓp)\text{max}(\ell_{p}) and a corresponding digital normalized Doppler spread max​(fp)\text{max}(f_{p}), satisfying the relations max​(ℓp)<<N\text{max}(\ell_{p})<<N and max​(fp)<<N\text{max}(f_{p})<<N.

Let us start by pointing out that the channel impulse response given in equation (1) can also be represented in the DD domain [16] as

h⁡(τ,ν)=∑p=0Php​δ​(τ−τp)​δ​(ν−νp),h(\tau,\nu)=\sum_{p=0}^{P}h_{p}\delta(\tau-\tau_{p})\delta(\nu-\nu_{p}),\vskip-2.15277pt (51)

which for a finite number PP of paths, and under the aforementioned bounding assumption on delay and Doppler parameters, can be rewritten as

h⁡(τ,ν)=∑k=0Kτ−1∑d=0Dν−1hk,d​δ​(τ−τk)​δ​(ν−νd),h(\tau,\nu)=\sum_{k=0}^{K_{\tau}-1}\sum_{d=0}^{D_{\nu}-1}h_{k,d}\delta(\tau-\tau_{k})\delta(\nu-\nu_{d}), (52)

where KτK_{\tau} and DνD_{\nu} are numbers large enough to define a sufficiently fine grid discretizing the region determined by the maximum delay and Doppler values.

Notice that if the resolution of such a grid is sufficiently fine, the only non-zero terms of the sum in equation (52) are those where both τk≈τp\tau_{k}\approx\tau_{p} and νd≈νp\nu_{d}\approx\nu_{p}, which in turn implies that estimating these radar parameters amounts to estimating the PP channel gains such that hk,d≠0h_{k,d}\neq 0. This suggests that the radar parameter estimation problem can be formulated as a canonical sparse signal recovery problem [55] as follows.

First, rewriting the time-continuous model of equation (52) in terms of the sampled equivalent in matrix form yields

𝐇¯≜∑k=0Kτ−1∑d=0Dν−1hk,d⋅𝚽k⋅𝛀fd⋅𝚷ℓk∈ℂN×N,\mathbf{\bar{H}}\triangleq\sum_{k=0}^{K_{\tau}-1}\sum_{d=0}^{D_{\nu}-1}h_{k,d}\cdot\mathbf{\Phi}_{k}\cdot\bm{\Omega}^{f_{d}}\cdot\mathbf{\Pi}^{\ell_{k}}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times N}, (53)

where we highlight that the model described by equation (53) is identical to the equivalent channel implicitly defined in equation (4), only with the summation rewritten over the DD grid, as opposed to the channel paths.

Then, the generalized receive signal model given in equation (27) can be rewritten as
𝐲=∑k=0Kτ−1∑d=0Dν−1𝚪k,d⋅𝐱⏟𝐞k,d∈ℂN×1⋅hk,d+𝐰~=𝐄⋅𝐡+𝐰~∈ℂN×1,\mathbf{y}\!=\!\!\sum_{k=0}^{K_{\tau}\!-\!1}\sum_{d=0}^{D_{\nu}-1}\!\!\underbrace{\mathbf{\Gamma}_{k,d}\cdot\mathbf{x}}_{\mathbf{e}_{k,d}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times 1}}\!\!\!\cdot h_{k,d}+\tilde{\mathbf{w}}=\mathbf{E}\cdot\mathbf{h}+\tilde{\mathbf{w}}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times 1},\vskip-6.45831pt (54a)
where we implicitly defined the vectors 𝐞k,d≜𝚪k,d⋅𝐱\mathbf{e}_{k,d}\triangleq\mathbf{\Gamma}_{k,d}\cdot\mathbf{x}, and explicitly identified the dictionary matrix 𝐄∈ℂN×Kτ​Dν\mathbf{E}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times K_{\tau}D_{\nu}}, and sparse channel vector 𝐡∈ℂKτ​Dν×1\mathbf{h}\in\mathbb{C}^{K_{\tau}D_{\nu}\times 1}, respectively defined as
𝐄≜[𝐞0,0,…,𝐞0,Dν−1,…,𝐞Kτ−1,0,…,𝐞Kτ−1,Dν−1],\mathbf{E}\!\triangleq\![\mathbf{e}_{0,0},\dots,\mathbf{e}_{0,D_{\nu}\!-\!1},\dots,\mathbf{e}_{K_{\tau}\!-\!1,0},\dots,\mathbf{e}_{K_{\tau}\!-\!1,D_{\nu}\!-\!1}],\vskip-4.30554pt (54b)
𝐡≜[h0,0,…,h0,Dν−1,…,hKτ−1,0,…,hKτ−1,Dν−1]𝖳.\mathbf{h}\!\triangleq\![h_{0,0},\dots,h_{0,D_{\nu}\!-\!1},\dots,h_{K_{\tau}\!-\!1,0},\dots,h_{K_{\tau}\!-\!1,D_{\nu}\!-\!1}]^{\mathsf{T}}\!\!\!. (54c)

In summary, the problem of estimating the set of radar parameters {τp,νp},∀p\{\tau_{p},\nu_{p}\},\forall p reduces to estimating the sparse channel vector 𝐡\mathbf{h}, with the delays and Doppler shifts obtained from the corresponding indices (k,d)(k,d) where hk,d≠0h_{k,d}\neq 0, given the received signal 𝐲\mathbf{y} and the dictionary matrix 𝐄\mathbf{E}. As a consequence of the approach, the assumption that PP is known is relaxed into the assumption that the channel paths are orthogonal in the delay-Doppler grid, such that PP can be unambiguously inferred from 𝐡\mathbf{h}. Finally, the method also implies the assumption that the transmit vector 𝐱\mathbf{x} is known at the radar receiver, which in turn translates to a number of possible scenarios [16], including those described below.

Monostatic RPE : A first scenario is the classic monostatic case, in which the BS processes round-trip signals reflected by surrounding scatters (targets) in order to extract their distances and velocities. Here, a main practical challenge is the self-interference caused by signals transmitted by the BS at the same time when reflected signals return. The issue is often ignored in related literature on OFDM- and OTFS-based monostatic RPE [11, 21], implying a strong and not entirely practical assumption that self-interference is perfectly avoided by FD technologies. To emphasize this point, it has been shown that AFDM has an advantage over OFDM and OTFS as it allows for the concentration of a single pilot symbol within a transmission block1818 18 Observe from equations (25) and (26) that unlike OFDM and OTFS, the AFDM receive signal occupies the entire time-frequency span even when a single entry in the transmit vector 𝐱\mathbf{x} is non-zero, such that concentrating piloting to a single symbol does not sacrifice the DoF of the estimator., as illustrated in Figure 2, with the corresponding self-interference mitigated via a simple analog dechirping and filtering operation [23]. We will therefore focus on this case.

User-centric RPE : In this case, the BS first transmits a pilot symbol vector used by the UE to perform RPE, and subsequently transmits data from which the UE proceeds to perform JCDE as described in Section III in order to track the channel and decode the information. Under the assumption that delay and Doppler shifts change at a rate slower than hph_{p} [56], the alternation of JCDE and RPE stages would enable the system to minimize the overhead associated with frequent pilot transmissions. Due to the lack of space, this scenario will not be further developed here, but we have shown in [28] that a well-designed JCDE algorithm is capable of tracking time-varying channels even without periodic pilot transmissions, as long as the BER of the system is maintained sufficiently low, e.g.e.g. via adequate channel coding. It is not difficult to envision that by combining the contribution of this article with the one in [28], the user-centric RPE scenario can be addressed.

Bistatic RPE : This refers to the case when passive receivers – could be BSs or UEs– which are placed at different locations with respect to the actively transmitting BS perform RPE using the received signals from the active BS [57, 58, 59, 60]. The scenario can be similar either to the latter user-centric case, if the passive receiver have no knowledge of the transmit vector 𝐱\mathbf{x} [60], or to the monostatic case, if 𝐱\mathbf{x} can be assumed known via pilot symbols, a preamble or a reference signal [57, 58, 59] to all the passive receivers. It is clear, therefore, that this scenario is a generalization of both, which is best addressed in a dedicated follow-up article, especially since the latter assumption – if BSs are considered – requires them to be interconnected via a fronthaul network, which in turn might be subjected to impairments such as delays, noise, capacity limitations etc.

For the rest of this manuscript, wlg and due to space limitations, we will focus on monostatic RPE.

IV-A Reference SotA Method: SBL via Expectation Maximization

Before we introduce our contribution, let us briefly review an effective SotA channel estimation approach, which is here adapted to solve the RPE problem, and which will be used as a reference for performance assessment. The technique, which is based on the SBL framework, was proposed in [31] for OTFS systems, but can also be employed to AFDM thanks to the unified model of Section II and the resulting sparse linear representation of equation (54). To see this, recall that the SBL approach models the sparse channel vector 𝐡\mathbf{h} as a parameterized Gaussian distribution of the form

f⁡(𝐡,𝚵)=∏m=0Kτ​Dν−11π​ξm​exp​(−|hm|2ξm),f(\mathbf{h};\mathbf{\Xi})=\prod_{m=0}^{K_{\tau}D_{\nu}-1}\frac{1}{\pi\xi_{m}}\text{exp}\bigg(-\frac{|h_{m}|^{2}}{\xi_{m}}\bigg), (55)

where ξm\xi_{m} denotes the unknown hyperparameter corresponding to the mm-th component of the vector 𝐡\mathbf{h}, collected into the matrix 𝚵≜diag​({ξm}m=0Kτ​Dν−1)∈ℝ+Kτ​Dν×Kτ​Dν\mathbf{\Xi}\triangleq\text{diag}\big(\{\xi_{m}\}_{m=0}^{K_{\tau}D_{\nu}-1}\big)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{K_{\tau}D_{\nu}\times K_{\tau}D_{\nu}}.

Then, estimates 𝐡^\mathbf{\!\hat{\;h}} of the sparse vector and its corresponding hyperparameter matrix 𝚵^\hat{\mathbf{\Xi}} are computed iteratively leveraging the EM method, which requires knowledge of the noise covariance matrix associated with the received signal model.

For the case of OTFS, from the definition of 𝐰~OTFS\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{\text{OTFS}} given just after equation (18) and under the assumption of rectangular pulse-shaping, we readily have

𝐑𝐰≜𝔼⁡[𝐰~OTFS⋅𝐰~OTFS𝖧]=𝔼⁡[[(𝐅M⊗𝐈K)​𝐰]⋅[(𝐅M⊗𝐈K)​𝐰]𝖧]\displaystyle\mathbf{R_{w}}\!\triangleq\!\mathbb{E}\Big[\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{\text{OTFS}}\!\cdot\!\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{\text{OTFS}}^{\mathsf{H}}\Big]\!\!=\!\mathbb{E}\Big[\big[(\mathbf{F}_{M}\!\otimes\!\mathbf{I}_{K})\mathbf{w}\big]\!\!\cdot\!\!\big[(\mathbf{F}_{M}\!\otimes\!\mathbf{I}_{K})\mathbf{w}\big]^{\mathsf{H}}\Big]
=(𝐅M⊗𝐈K)⋅N0​𝐈N⋅(𝐅M⊗𝐈K)𝖧=N0​[𝐅M​𝐅M𝖧⊗𝐈K​𝐈K𝖧]\displaystyle\hskip-249.72144pt=(\mathbf{F}_{M}\!\otimes\!\mathbf{I}_{K})\!\cdot\!{N_{0}}\mathbf{I}_{N}\!\cdot\!(\mathbf{F}_{M}\!\otimes\!\mathbf{I}_{K})^{\mathsf{H}}\!=\!{N_{0}}\Big[\mathbf{F}_{M}\mathbf{F}_{M}^{\mathsf{H}}\!\otimes\!\mathbf{I}_{K}\mathbf{I}_{K}^{\mathsf{H}}\Big]
=N0​[𝐈M⊗𝐈K​𝐈K𝖧]=N0​𝐈N∈ℂN×N.\hskip-65.8748pt={N_{0}}\Big[\mathbf{I}_{M}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{K}\mathbf{I}_{K}^{\mathsf{H}}\Big]={N_{0}}\mathbf{I}_{N}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times N}. (56)

In turn, taking into account the definition of 𝐰~AFDM\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{\text{AFDM}} given after equation (25), we have for the AFDM case

𝐑𝐰≜𝔼⁡[𝐰~AFDM⋅𝐰~AFDM𝖧]=𝔼⁡[[(𝚲2​𝐅N​𝚲1)​𝐰]⋅[(𝚲2​𝐅N​𝚲1)​𝐰]𝖧]\displaystyle\mathbf{R_{w}}\!\triangleq\!\mathbb{E}\Big[\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{\text{AFDM}}\!\cdot\!\tilde{\mathbf{w}}_{\text{AFDM}}^{\mathsf{H}}\Big]\!\!=\!\mathbb{E}\Big[\!\big[(\!\mathbf{\Lambda}_{2}\mathbf{F}_{\!N}\mathbf{\Lambda}_{1}\!)\mathbf{w}\big]\!\!\cdot\!\!\big[(\!\mathbf{\Lambda}_{2}\mathbf{F}_{\!N}\mathbf{\Lambda}_{1}\!)\mathbf{w}\big]^{\mathsf{H}}\!\Big]
=𝔼⁡[[(𝚲2​𝐅N​𝚲1)​𝐰]⋅[𝐰𝖧​(𝚲2​𝐅N​𝚲1)𝖧]]\displaystyle\hskip-249.72144pt=\mathbb{E}\Big[\big[(\!\mathbf{\Lambda}_{2}\mathbf{F}_{\!N}\mathbf{\Lambda}_{1}\!)\mathbf{w}\big]\!\cdot\!\big[\mathbf{w}^{\mathsf{H}}(\!\mathbf{\Lambda}_{2}\mathbf{F}_{\!N}\mathbf{\Lambda}_{1}\!)^{\mathsf{H}}\big]\Big]
=(𝚲2​𝐅N​𝚲1)⋅N0​𝐈N⋅(𝚲2​𝐅N​𝚲1)𝖧=N0​𝐈N∈ℂN×N.\displaystyle\hskip-249.72144pt=(\!\mathbf{\Lambda}_{2}\mathbf{F}_{\!N}\mathbf{\Lambda}_{1}\!)\!\cdot\!{N_{0}}\mathbf{I}_{N}\!\cdot\!(\!\mathbf{\Lambda}_{2}\mathbf{F}_{\!N}\mathbf{\Lambda}_{1}\!)^{\mathsf{H}}\!=\!{N_{0}}\mathbf{I}_{N}\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times N}.

A pseudocode summary of the SBL-based RPE scheme is offered in Algorithm 2.

IV-B Proposed Method: PDA-based Message Passing Estimator

In this section, we propose a novel PDA-based RPE scheme designed under the assumption that the prior distributions of the elements h^m\hat{h}_{m} of the sparse channel vector estimates 𝐡^\mathbf{\!\hat{\;h}} are of Bernoulli-Gaussian type. In other words, we model the unknown channel to be estimated at the ii-th iteration of the proposed scheme as

h^m(i)∼phm​(hm,𝜽(i)),\hat{h}_{m}^{(i)}\sim p_{\,\text{h}_{m}}(\text{h}_{m};\bm{\theta}^{(i)}),\vskip-8.61108pt (58)

with

phm​(hm,𝜽(i))≜(−ρ(i))​δ​(hm)+ρ(i)​𝒞​𝒩​(hm,h¯(i),σ¯(i)),\!\!p_{\,\text{h}_{m}}(\text{h}_{m};\bm{\theta}^{(i)})\triangleq\!(1\!-\!{\rho}^{(i)})\delta(h_{m})\!+\!{\rho}^{(i)}\mathcal{CN}\big(h_{m};{\bar{h}}^{(i)},{\bar{\sigma}}^{(i)}\big),\!\!\vskip-2.15277pt (59)

where 𝜽(i)≜[ρ(i),h¯(i),σ¯(i)]\bm{\theta}^{(i)}\triangleq[{\rho}^{(i)},{\bar{h}}^{(i)},{\bar{\sigma}}^{(i)}] carries all three parameters of the distribution, namely, sparsity rate, mean and variance.

As implied by the notation, the parameter vector 𝜽(i)\bm{\theta}^{(i)} must be updated iteratively, which in similarity to the SBL approach of [31] can be accomplished via the EM algorithm. Unlike the aforementioned SotA method, however, the estimates of 𝐡\mathbf{h} in the proposed scheme are obtained via a message-passing algorithm, which is described in the sequel.

For later convenience, we define the soft replica (i.e., tentative estimate) of hmh_{m} as {h^m(i)}\big\{\hat{h}_{m}^{(i)}\big\} such that its MSE can be expressed as

σ^h:m2​(i)≜𝔼hm[|hm−h^m(i)|2].\hat{\sigma}_{h:m}^{2(i)}\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{\text{h}_{m}}\big[|h_{m}-\hat{h}_{m}^{(i)}|^{2}\big]. (60)

Following steps similar to those in Section III-A, we have

IV-B1 Soft IC

The soft IC expression corresponding to an estimate of hmh_{m}, is given by

𝐲~h:m(i)=𝐲−∑q≠m𝐞qh^q(i)=𝐞mhm+∑q≠mKτ​Dν(𝐞q​hq−𝐞q​h^q(i))+𝐰~⏞residual interference+noise component,\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{h:m}^{(i)}\!=\mathbf{y}\!-\!\!\!\sum_{q\neq m}\!\!\mathbf{e}_{q}\hat{h}_{q}^{(i)}\!=\!\mathbf{e}_{m}h_{m}\!+\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\overbrace{\sum_{q\neq m}^{K_{\tau}D_{\nu}}(\mathbf{e}_{q}h_{q}\!-\!\mathbf{e}_{q}\hat{h}_{q}^{(i)})\!+\!\tilde{\mathbf{w}}}^{\text{residual interference+noise component}}\!\!\!,\!\! (61)

where 𝐞m\mathbf{e}_{m} is the mm-th column of the dictionary matrix 𝐄\mathbf{E}.

It follows from the central limit theorem (CLT) that, under large-system conditions, the residual interference-plus-noise component can be approximated by a multivariate complex Gaussian variate. In other words, the vector Gaussian approximation (VGA) can be applied such that the conditional PDF of the beliefs 𝐲~h:m(i)\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{h:m}^{(i)}, given hmh_{m}, can be expressed as

𝐲~h:m(i)∼py|hm(y|hm)∝exp[−(y−𝐞mhm)𝖧𝚺m−1​(i)(y−𝐞mhm)],\!\!\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{h:m}^{(i)}\!\!\sim\!p_{\textbf{y}|\text{h}_{m}}\!(\textbf{y}|h_{m}\!)\!\propto\!\text{exp}\!\Big[\!-\!\big(\!\textbf{y}\!-\!\mathbf{e}_{m}h_{m}\!\big)^{\mathsf{H}}\mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1(i)}_{m}\!\big(\!\textbf{y}\!-\!\mathbf{e}_{m}h_{m}\!\big)\!\Big]\!,\!\!\! (62)

where y is an auxiliary variable, and the conditional covariance matrix 𝚺m(i)\mathbf{\Sigma}_{m}^{(i)} is given by
